agent_notes: Revised after the reviewer's request: the dramatic layer no longer says the teaching 'is not mine alone'; the teaching is the speaker's own, 'my teaching, the words of my mouth'. The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew numbering (KJV 78:0) and is translated as part of the verse. 'Maskil' is a transliterated genre label in the literal layer; 'instructive poem' (from sakal) is a common reading, not a certainty.

STEPBible glosses תּוֹרָה as 'instruction'. I kept 'torah' in the literal layer and 'teaching' in the dramatic one: the poem uses the word for a recited history, not statute, so the KJV/ASV 'law' narrows it.

history.note: [should_fix] Remove 'is not mine alone, but it'. Keep the teaching as the speaker's own ('my teaching, the words of my mouth'). (PS.78.1: "הַאֲזִינָה עַמִּי תּוֹרָתִי הַטּוּ אָזְנְכֶם לְאִמְרֵי־פִי")

agent_notes: שְׂדֵה־צֹעַן: I glossed 'field/country of Zoan' and treated it as apposition to 'land of Egypt', as Radak and Metzudat David do. Zoan = Tanis is the standard identification (the packet's registry also marks it loc.zoan); the claim about the Ramesside royal seat is my own background knowledge and I left it unsourced.

Reviewer request addressed: the commentary no longer says 'only'. נֵד 'heap' is a rare word: Exod 15:8, Josh 3:13 and 3:16, Isa 17:11, Ps 33:7 (כַּנֵּד) and here, by my count from memory of the concordance; I did not claim a total, and left 'sources' empty for the list.

The five English versions agree except BBE, which paraphrases 'massed together on this side and on that' and adds a 'both sides' idea the Hebrew does not state. I followed KJV/ASV structure for the literal layer but kept 'sea' without the article, as the Hebrew has none.
Gloss of token 4 corrected from STEPBible 'and he made to stand up' to 'and he made [them] stand': the Hiphil of נצב is causative, and the object is the following 'waters'.

history.note: [should_fix] Add Ps 33:7 to the list of occurrences of נֵד, or drop 'only'. (PS.78.13: "וַיַּצֶּב־מַיִם כְּמוֹ־נֵד"; Ps 33:7 also has "כֹּנֵס כַּנֵּד מֵי הַיָּם")

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: 'pillar' removed from the dramatic layer. The Hebrew says cloud and 'light of fire'; the 'pillars' (עמוד) are in Exod 13:21 and in Radak and Malbim here, not in the verse.

history.note: [should_fix] Remove 'pillar' from the dramatic layer, for example 'a canopy of shade in the glare', so that it matches the Hebrew and your own commentary. (PS.78.14: "וַיַּנְחֵם בֶּעָנָן יוֹמָם וְכָל־הַלַּיְלָה בְּאוֹר אֵשׁ": with the cloud by day, with a light of fire all night)
[consider] Either add Ibn Ezra's point to the note or drop him from its sources. (PS.78.14: "וְכָל־הַלַּיְלָה בְּאוֹר אֵשׁ")

agent_notes: יְבַקַּע is an imperfect (piel) among narrative wayyiqtols. I rendered it as a past event in the dramatic layer and left it present-tense-neutral ('He splits') in the literal layer. Radak on Psalm 78:15 reads it as an imperfect standing for the past. KJV, ASV and Webster use the past; YLT uses the present. The same verse has a plural noun (צֻרִים, rocks) and the singular 'rock' in v. 16 and v. 20.

כִּתְהֹמוֹת רַבָּה has a plural noun with a feminine singular adjective. Ibn Ezra and Radak (both on Psalm 78:15) compare 'daughters of Zaanah' (Gen 49:22 as 'bənot ṣaʿadah'). I kept it literal as 'like deeps, abundant'. Neither commentator's parallel is repeated in the translation.

STEPBible glosses בֵּאלֹהִים 'against God' and tags both אֵל and אֱלֹהִים as deity.yhwh. I kept 'against God' for the verb דִּבֶּר + בְּ, a hostile use, and translated אֵל as 'God' in the quoted speech. The speakers use the generic divine word, not the name YHWH.

Revised after the reviewer's request: the two examples are now separate. Radak ties 'bread of the mighty' (Ps 78:25) to the manna, and 'he gave his might into captivity' (v. 61) to the ark, which he says could not be understood without 1 Samuel; Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra give the ark example too. Rashi's reading of 'parable' as the words of Torah is mentioned as a separate view. The verse-number citations (78:25, 78:61) are mine; the commentators quote the phrases.

history.note: [should_fix] Separate the two examples: the manna as 'bread of the mighty' (Radak), and the ark in v. 61, which can only be understood from 1 Samuel (Radak, Metzudat David). (Radak on 78:2: "לחם אבירים אכל איש שהוא אומר על המן כמו חידה ויתן לשבי עוזו שהוא אומר על הארון ולא היו מבינים זה לולי שכתב בספר שמואל")

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses שְׁאֵר as 'meat'. I kept 'flesh/meat' in the gloss and the literal layer; Rashi on Psalm 78:20 gives בָּשָׂר. KJV 'flesh' is correct here. The Ibn Ezra comment on the order of events (manna before the rock at Rephidim, Exodus 16 versus 17) is a real tension I only mention in the commentary of v. 20 and v. 24 briefly; I do not adjudicate it.

וַיִּתְעַבָּר is a hithpael of עָבַר 'to cross over, overflow' in the sense 'to burst out in fury'. STEPBible 'and he was furious' is fine. I corrected nothing here. נִשְּׂקָה is niphal of שׂלק (kindle), a hapax verb root per STEPBible; Rashi on Psalm 78:21 links it to הִשִּׂיקוּ in Ezekiel 39:9. KJV 'against' is an interpretation; the Hebrew has בְּ 'in'.

history.note: [consider] Use 'anger rose in Israel' in the dramatic layer, or soften the remark on the KJV. (PS.78.21: "וְגַם־אַף עָלָה בְיִשְׂרָאֵל")

agent_notes: KJV, ASV and Webster render the wayyiqtols as pluperfects ('Though he had commanded'). That follows Ibn Ezra and Radak on Psalm 78:23 ('he had already commanded'). The Hebrew has plain narrative forms. I kept simple past in both layers and said so in the commentary; the reader can hear a flashback in the dramatic layer without a stated tense shift.

דְּגַן שָׁמַיִם: STEPBible gives 'grain of heaven'. KJV 'corn of heaven' is the older English 'corn' for grain, which a modern reader misreads as maize. The Targum's עִבּוּר (produce) is not used in my translation.

אַבִּירִים is rendered 'mighty ones' in the literal layer, a plural that the packet's KJV, Webster and Targum read as 'angels'. Rashi and Radak also take it as heavenly beings (Radak: the skies), with Rashi's second reading 'limbs' (אֵיבָרִים). The Hebrew word itself does not say 'angels'; the dramatic layer keeps the ambiguity ('the mighty ones') rather than naming angels.

צֵידָה: STEPBible 'food', YLT 'venison', KJV/Webster 'meat/food'. The root is צוד 'to hunt', so provisions taken on a journey or game. I kept 'provisions' to carry both senses; a gloss correction from STEPBible's 'food'.

יַסַּע is the verb for pulling up tent pegs and breaking camp (nasa'), so the wind 'sets out'. KJV 'caused to blow' and BBE 'sent' lose this. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Malbim in the packet read the pair of winds as a miracle, because a south-east wind would carry quail away from Israel (Malbim); the Hebrew itself only names the winds.

The suffix in מַחֲנֵהוּ and לְמִשְׁכְּנֹתָיו is singular 'his'. YLT reads it as God's own camp, KJV/ASV/Webster as 'their' camp. Context (the quail fall for Israel) makes 'their' the sense, but I kept the singular 'his' in the literal layer and put the choice in the commentary. The object of 'made fall' is not stated; the quail of v. 27 are understood.

history.note: [consider] Optionally trim 'by the fire' and keep the repeated telling. (PS.78.3: "אֲשֶׁר שָׁמַעְנוּ וַנֵּדָעֵם וַאֲבוֹתֵינוּ סִפְּרוּ־לָנוּ")

agent_notes: זָרוּ gloss: STEPBible 'had become estranged'. I glossed it 'turned aside' with the root meaning 'be strange'. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as 'had not yet been disgusted', linking to זָרָא 'loathsome' in Num 11:20; the commentary cites this only as Ibn Ezra's association. The pointing of the verse's last words is a clause, not a new sentence, hence the continuation into v. 31.

מִשְׁמַנֵּיהֶם: 'fat ones' (from שמן, oil/fat) versus the adjective 'vigorous, sturdy' that Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take. I kept 'their fat ones' in the literal layer and wrote 'the strongest' in the dramatic layer. בַּחוּרֵי: 'young men' versus 'chosen' (Rashi, Metzudat David); the root בחר gives both, and KJV/Webster 'chosen men' follows the second. Rashi's identification of the 'fat' with the elders is a claim about Num 11 that I did not repeat.

הֶאֱמִינוּ בְּ takes ב 'in': 'believed in his wonders', not KJV/Webster 'for his wondrous works', which makes the wonders the reason, not the object of trust. The packet commentators (Radak, Meiri, Malbim) tie the verse to the spies episode, but this is their reading of the 'all this', not something the verse says.

אִם with a perfect verb: the commentators (Radak, Meiri) take it as 'whenever, when', as KJV/ASV/Webster do. The literal layer keeps 'if he killed them' and the commentary explains why 'when' is the right sense. Rashi reads the repentance as insincere already at v. 34; the next two verses support that, so I follow the same reading in the dramatic layer but only as the setup for v. 36.

I kept 'God' for אֱלֹהִים and אֵל in the dramatic layer, since the divine name YHWH does not occur in these verses; only 'LORD' is used when the text has YHWH. The packet's entity link of אֵל עֶלְיוֹן is to the generic LORD; that is the registry's identification, not a claim about the word.

וַיְפַתּוּהוּ: piel of פתה 'entice, persuade, dupe'. KJV/ASV/Webster 'flatter', YLT 'deceive'. 'Seduce' would be too strong; I chose 'tried to coax/deceive', with 'coaxed' in the dramatic layer. The verb is a past narrative form followed by an imperfect, both of which I rendered in the past.

Rashi on this verse is a long midrashic comment about the evil impulse and resurrection; I did not use it for the sense of the verse. The perfect/imperfect forms (יְכַפֵּר, יַשְׁחִית) are read as habitual, following Ibn Ezra's note on the tense.

The five English versions agree on 'flesh'; BBE renders רוּחַ as 'breath'. Hebrew רוּחַ can be wind or breath, and the pun between the two is intended; I keep 'wind' in the literal layer and use both in the dramatic one.

Revised after the reviewer's request: the contrast with the myths of the Greeks is attributed to Malbim alone. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read 'their children' as the children of 'our fathers', that is, our brothers in Israel who have not received the tradition; that is what the commentary now credits to Radak.

history.note: [should_fix] Give the contrast with the Greeks' myths to Malbim alone, and drop 'and the other medieval commentators'. (Malbim on 78:4: "הבלי היונים וחדותיהם הם מכחידים אותם מבניהם, כי לא ימסרו אותם רק לזקניהם וכהניהם"; Radak: "חייבים אנו היודעים להזכיר להם")

agent_notes: הִתְווּ (hitvu) is a hapax-like form of תָּוָה 'to mark'. STEPBible glosses it 'they pained'; I follow the 'mark a limit' reading (Radak, Meiri, Malbim; Rashi 'demand a sign') and render 'they set a mark on'. KJV 'limited' is the same reading. ASV 'provoked' and BBE 'gave pain' follow the other tradition (from תָּוָה II/ תכה, to grieve), which I mention but do not adopt.

Revised per the reviewer request: Zoan is identified as Djanet (Greek Tanis), the Egyptian name given as background and not attributed to a commentator. The location in the northeastern Delta, in the region of Goshen, is also background. Meiri is cited only for what he says: that 'field of Zoan' means 'land of Zoan', like 'field of Aram'.

STEPBible glosses 'when' for אֲשֶׁר and 'performed' for שָׂם. I read אֲשֶׁר as 'how' (the five English versions mostly say 'how'), continuing the 'remembering' clause of v.42, and שָׂם as 'he set/placed', the verb the Hebrew chooses; KJV 'wrought' and BBE 'done' are looser.

Malbim's distinction between signs (אותות) in Egypt and wonders (מופתים) in the field of Zoan is his own reading of the plague cycle, not the plain sense of a poetic parallel. Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra take the two halves as synonymous, and I follow that in the commentary.

history.note: [should_fix] Replace 'Tjaru or Tanis' with 'Djanet (Greek Tanis)'. Mark the location near Goshen as background, not as Meiri's view. (PS.78.43: "וּמוֹפְתָיו בִּשְׂדֵה־צֹעַן"; Meiri: "שדה צוען פי׳ ארץ צוען כמו שדה ארם")

agent_notes: חֲנָמַל is a hapax of uncertain meaning. Rashi takes it as a kind of locust, Ibn Ezra as hailstones, Radak and Meiri (citing Saadia) as hard frost or ice. STEPBible's 'a flood' is unsupported by any commentary in the packet. I translate 'frost' in the dramatic layer and leave a transliteration in the literal layer.

לָרְשָׁפִים: I read 'bolts of fire' (Exod 9:24, as Rashi's plain sense, Radak, Meiri). The link to the Canaanite plague-god Resheph is my own context, not from the packet commentaries; I flagged it without citing a source.

מַלְאֲכֵי רָעִים: the five English versions split between 'evil angels' (KJV, Webster), 'angels of evil' (ASV) and 'evil messengers' (YLT). Radak and Meiri read it as an unbound construction, 'evil angels', i.e. the plagues themselves as God's envoys; Ibn Ezra reads 'messengers of calamities'. I kept the literal 'messengers of evils' and let the commentary carry the debate. STEPBible glosses מַלְאֲכֵי as 'angels of' and רָעִים as 'calamities'; I gloss 'messengers of' because the word is the ordinary Hebrew for any envoy.

The Targum's 'two hundred and fifty plagues' (מָאתָן וְחַמְשִׁין מְחָן) is a Targumic expansion not in the Hebrew; I do not use it. Meiri's reading that the verse compresses the five unnamed plagues into five terms (anger, fury, indignation, trouble, a band of messengers) is his own and I mention it only as a tradition.

וְחַיָּתָם is disputed: Rashi 'their bodies', Ibn Ezra and Radak 'their life' (= נַפְשָׁם), Metzudat Zion and some in Radak 'their livestock' (חַיָּה as animals). I translate 'their life' in the literal layer and note the livestock reading, since the pestilence (דֶּבֶר) in Exodus 9 struck cattle. The dramatic layer keeps 'life', which also fits the death of the firstborn in the next verse.
The KJV 'spared not' softens לֹא־חָשַׂךְ, 'did not hold back'; I keep the plain verb. 'Soul' stays because נֶפֶשׁ is the person's life-breath.

אוֹנִים: STEPBible glosses 'manly vigor'; Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion tie it to Genesis 49:3 (רֵאשִׁית אוֹנִי, Reuben) and Hosea 12:9, 'strength, vigor'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the first sign of the father's vigor. I render 'first of vigor' and keep the procreative sense in the commentary.

history.note: [consider] Rephrase it as a change in the order of the phrases inside the second clause, or drop the remark. (KJV PS.78.52: "But made his own people to go forth like sheep, and guided them in the wilderness like a flock.")

agent_notes: Verb of the last clause: the text has the object first (וְאֶת־אוֹיְבֵיהֶם) and the verb כִּסָּה with 'the sea' as subject; the literal layer keeps that word order. KJV 'overwhelmed' is its own word for 'covered'.

גְּבוּל קָדְשׁוֹ and הַר־זֶה are disputed: Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David read the border as the land of Israel and 'this mountain' as the Temple mount, with Radak and Ibn Ezra raising the question of when the psalm could say 'this'; Ibn Ezra's second reading takes the mountain as the hill country with Lebanon. I keep 'territory of his holiness' and 'this mountain' open, and the commentary names both readings. The verb קָנְתָה is feminine, agreeing with יְמִינוֹ (right hand), not with הַר (masculine), so 'his right hand acquired' is the construction; this is my own grammatical observation.

history.note: [consider] Align the commentary with the note: Ibn Ezra = Jerusalem/Moriah; Radak and Metzudat David = the land of Israel. (Ibn Ezra on 78:54: "ויביאם אל גבול קדשו - ירושלם"; "הר זה - הוא הר המוריה")

agent_notes: וַיַּפִּילֵם בְּחֶבֶל נַחֲלָה: the 'them' is ambiguous. Radak gives two readings: it is Israel whom God made fall (i.e. assigned by lot, cf. Josh 13:6), or it is the nations whom God made fall by the sword in their own land. Metzudat David takes the lot. The Hebrew uses the causative of 'fall' for both casting lots and felling; I keep 'made them fall' and put the ambiguity in the commentary. The KJV 'divided them an inheritance' picks the lot reading silently.

Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all place this verse in the time of the judges, after Joshua and the elders; Ibn Ezra says it begins the telling of how Ephraim rebelled. I follow the former because the verse has no named subject and continues the plural 'they' of the whole psalm.

history.note: [consider] Say 'compare אֵל עֶלְיוֹן in Gen 14:19' (or v. 35 of this psalm). (PS.78.56: "אֶת־אֱלֹהִים עֶלְיוֹן")

agent_notes: וַיִּסֹּגוּ: STEPBible lemma is סוּג with a Niphal form; Ibn Ezra says it is Niphal of סגג, like וַיִּכֹּנוּ. 'Turned back' is the meaning in all five versions. קֶשֶׁת רְמִיָּה: Ibn Ezra offers two readings (רמיה as an adjective of the bow, or as a noun 'shooter', as in רֹמֵי קֶשֶׁת). I keep 'bow of deceit' and the sense Rashi gives, that the bow does not send the arrow where the archer aims.
Targum renders בבמותם as 'with their libations' (בנסכיהון), reading the high places as cultic acts; the Hebrew is the same בָּמָה as elsewhere, 'high place'. I do not follow the Targum here.

וַיִּתְעַבָּר: Hithpael of עבר, 'he passed over [the limit]', here 'he was furious'. YLT 'sheweth Himself wroth' is the literal reflexive. Ibn Ezra's gloss ('he crossed the bound of anger') is my source for the etymological note; Malbim makes it a different definition (anger that passes the border to those who did not sin). The KJV 'abhorred' for וַיִּמְאַס is stronger than the root's usual 'reject, spurn'.

מִשְׁכַּן שִׁלוֹ: the Hebrew has a construct 'tabernacle of Shiloh'; the next phrase אֹהֶל שִׁכֵּן בָּאָדָם is in apposition, 'the tent [that] he had pitched among humankind'. שִׁכֵּן is a Piel perfect used as a relative clause without אֲשֶׁר. Ibn Ezra's note that it is called 'tent' because the ark stood without a roof is his own and I report it as such.

history.note: [consider] Attribute the quote 'the ark of your strength' to Ps 132:8. (Ibn Ezra on 78:61: "הוא הארון אתה וארון עזך דרשו את ה' ועוזו")

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the BDB source is removed. The note on the verb cites Metzudat Zion (ויסגר = מסר) and Radak; the note on התעבר is my own reading, with no source.

history.note: [should_fix] Replace the BDB source with a packet commentary that supports the note (for example Ibn Ezra on 78:59, 'crossed the bound of anger'), or leave sources empty. (PS.78.62 packet commentaries: Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion, Malbim, Targum; no lexicon)

agent_notes: הוּלָּלוּ (Pual of הלל) is read as 'were praised', i.e. given the wedding song; Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all tie it to הלולא (wedding celebration). Rashi also notes that the rabbis applied the verse to Nadab and Abihu and says he is not at ease with that, since the verse is already speaking of Shiloh.

מִתְרוֹנֵן is a hapax-like Hitpolel of רנן/רון; I follow Rashi (rousing himself with shouting, from רִנָּה) and render 'ringing out', not KJV 'shouteth by reason of wine'. The preposition מִן can mean 'from (the effect of)' or 'because of'; I keep 'from wine' in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer take the 'shaking off' sense.

The rendering of אָחוֹר as 'backward' stays literal. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Meiri and the Targum read it as the tumours (עפולים/טחורים) of 1 Sam 5:6, a link made by the commentators; the verse itself does not name the illness, so the dramatic layer only hints at a blow struck at the back.

Reviewer request addressed: the BDB source is removed; the note on מאס now cites Metzudat David and Rashi from the packet. 'Tent of Joseph' is read as Shiloh in Ephraim's territory, as Rashi and Metzudat David read it; the verse itself does not name Shiloh.

history.note: [should_fix] Remove the BDB source, or cite a packet commentary (for example Metzudat David: 'מאז מאס במשכן שילה'). (PS.78.67 packet commentaries: Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David, Malbim, Targum; no lexicon)

agent_notes: רָמִים is a bare participle, 'the high ones'. Ibn Ezra and Radak supply 'palaces' (cf. KJV 'high palaces'), Rashi and Metzudat David take it as the heavens. I keep 'the high [heights]' in the literal layer and choose the heavens in the dramatic layer, paired with 'the earth'. The Targum's 'horn of a unicorn' is a separate reading (רמים read as ראמים) that I mention in the commentary.

כִּסְלָם: STEPBible 'confidence'. I kept it. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all gloss it as trust/hope; Rashi cites Job 31:24. The homograph כֶּסֶל 'folly' is a different root and is not meant here.

עָלוֹת is glossed 'nursing ewes' (from עול, suckling young; so Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion). KJV 'great with young' rests on a different sense of the root and is probably wrong here; the verbal notion in Gen 33:13 and Isa 40:11 is of ewes with suckling young.

Blocker addressed: the claim that v. 52 speaks of Moses and Aaron is removed. The commentary now says that in v. 52 God himself made his people set out like sheep and led them like a flock, and that here the shepherd's task passes to David.

Verse 71's 'ewes with young' and the v. 72 shepherd imagery follow Rashi and Meiri on v. 71-72, a midrashic tradition about David's care for different animals. I cite it as tradition, not as what the Hebrew says.
First word glossed 'and he shepherded them': the verb is from רעה 'to shepherd', which also means 'to feed'. KJV 'fed' keeps only half; YLT 'ruleth' keeps only the royal sense.

history.note: [blocker] Remove the claim that verse 52 speaks of Moses and Aaron. If you keep the contrast, say that in v. 52 God himself shepherded the flock and that in vv. 70-72 he hands the shepherd's task to David. (PS.78.52: "וַיַּסַּע כַּצֹּאן עַמּוֹ וַיְנַהֲגֵם כַּעֵדֶר בַּמִּדְבָּר": he (God) made his people set out like sheep and led them like a flock)

agent_notes: נֶאֶמְנָה is feminine singular, agreeing with רוּחוֹ (spirit, feminine), not with 'generation'. Glossed 'was made firm/faithful'. Radak offers two readings (thought not firm with God, or 'amanah' as pact); I follow the first.

Hard verse: the historical referent of Ephraim's retreat is disputed. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David connect it to 1 Chr 7:21 (the Ephraimite raid on Gath) or to an early exit from Egypt; Ibn Ezra and Malbim read it as Shiloh's fall in Eli's day or as Ephraim standing for the northern kingdom. I do not choose between them in the translation and present the options in the commentary. 'Armed' for נוֹשְׁקֵי is as the commentators (Radak, Metzudat Zion), the construct chain נוֹשְׁקֵי רוֹמֵי־קֶשֶׁת is rendered 'equipped, shooters of the bow'; the five English versions split on whether this is one phrase or two.

'Turned' is without an object in the Hebrew. 'Turned back' (KJV, ASV) supplies 'back' by reading the verb as retreat; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David read 'turned the neck/back'. I bracket 'back' in the literal layer.

history.note: [consider] Give the Shiloh/Eli reading to Malbim, and Ibn Ezra the figurative one. (Ibn Ezra on 78:9: "שהפכו עורף ביום קרב, משל בעבור שלא שמרו ברית אלהים")
